title: Where Will AbbVie Stock Be in 5 Years? Its 2 Immunology Blockbusters Are Still Growing 20%-Plus per Year - The Globe and Mail
content: AbbVie’s two growth pillars, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, should rack up more than $31 billion in sales this year, and neither should experience a patent cliff in the next five years. The company also boasts attractive pipeline candidates like Zumilokibart and ABBV-295. Over the past five years, AbbVie(NYSE:ABBV) has more than tripled the S&P 500's total return, despite losing patent exclusivity for its biggest growth driver, Humira, an immunology medicine. The company's ability to overcome the loss of Humira, the best-selling drug in the industry's history, speaks volumes about its underlying business. But where might AbbVie be headed over the next five years? Let's see whether the drugmaker can continue beating the market. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » AbbVie's core growth drivers in recent years have been Skyrizi and Rinvoq, two immunology drugs that have earned numerous indications overlapping with those of Humira. In fact, these two drugs have demonstrated superior efficacy compared to Humira across several indications. For instance, in a Phase 3 study in certain patients with plaque psoriasis, AbbVie pitted Skyrizi against Humira, and the former performed better. Rinvoq also beat Humira in studies in some patients with rheumatoid arthritis. It's no wonder, then, that these two medicines already combine to generate more than Humira's $21.2 billion peak annual sales. Through Sept. 30, Skyrizi's revenue was $15.8 billion, up 25.6% year over year. Rinvoq's sales came in at $7.4 billion, 23.9% higher than the year-ago period. What's more, both have secured several expansions this year and should win more over the next five years. And neither will lose patent exclusivity until at least 2033. Note that they have made it a habit to exceed expectations. AbbVie expects them to combine for more than $31 billion in sales this year. It had initially set a $31 billion combined target for 2027 (and even that 2027 guidance was $4 billion above a previous one). True, the competitive landscape will evolve over the next few years. That could be a problem for AbbVie. But even with that caveat, we can expect Skyrizi and Rinvoq to continue performing well over the medium term. Five years is enough time for AbbVie to launch several new products that will help it improve its financial results and overcome challenges, including government-led drug price negotiations in the U.S., which could reduce sales for some of its products. The pharmaceutical leader boasts several promising candidates investors should keep an eye on. One of the most promising is zumilokibart, an investigational medicine for eczema. Here's why this candidate looks particularly attractive. According to some estimates, the eczema drug market was valued at $21 billion last year and could rise to $46 billion by 2034. It's a highly competitive industry, but zumilokibart has shown promising efficacy data while also benefiting from a very convenient twice-a-year maintenance dosing schedule, something no currently approved medicine in the U.S. offers. If zumilokibart performs well in Phase 3 studies and earns approval within the next five years, it could help strengthen AbbVie's portfolio and extend its lead in immunology. Another important candidate AbbVie is working on is ABBV-295, an investigational weight-loss medicine, perhaps one of the fastest-growing therapeutic areas in the industry. AbbVie licensed ABBV-295 from a Denmark-based company. The weight loss drug market might be worth $150 billion by 2035, up from $15 billion in 2024. AbbVie's ABBV-295 is being investigated as a long-acting treatment and, if approved, may be administered once per month. Investors should also keep track of ABBV-295's progress over the next few years, and these two candidates are only the tip of the iceberg. AbbVie is developing many more brand-new drugs and could have an even stronger portfolio by 2031. In the meantime, the company expects no major loss of patent exclusivity through the end of the decade. The market is well aware of AbbVie's excellent prospects. That's why the drugmaker's shares have crushed broader equities this year. But is the stock too expensive? Not in my view. AbbVie is currently trading at 18.5x forward earnings, versus an average of 19.2x for healthcare stocks. One might argue that AbbVie is worth a premium over its peers, especially those in the pharmaceutical industry. Many drugmakers will face major patent cliffs by 2030, and few post sales and earnings growth as consistently as AbbVie's. Further, AbbVie has an outstanding dividend program, having increased its payouts for 55 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King (a company with 50 or more consecutive dividend increases). Given all that, I'd value AbbVie slightly above 20x forward earnings. So, at current levels, the stock looks like a steal. title: What Led ABBV's Oncology Franchise to Return to Growth in Q3? - The Globe and Mail
content: AbbVie’s ABBV oncology franchise returned to growth in the third quarter of 2026 after a series of year-over-year declines in the past quarters. The segment’s sales rose 0.9% on an operational basis to $1.7 billion, after reporting a 2.4% decline in the previous quarter and a 3% drop in the first quarter. Overall, the franchise accounted for 9.7% of the company’s total revenues. The improvement came as a surprise, with analysts and investors largely expecting oncology sales to remain flat or slip slightly. Though Imbruvica sales continued to be a drag on the business, it was offset by higher sales of Venclexta and newer cancer treatments. These products helped lift the segment back into positive territory, although growth remained modest. The biggest growth contributor within AbbVie’s oncology portfolio remained Venclexta, which recorded sales of $803 million, up 10.7% year over year. Growth was particularly strong in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), where combination use with BTK inhibitors has become a preferred fixed-duration treatment approach globally. In contrast, Imbruvica sales declined 26.1% year over year to $522 million. AbbVie attributed the weakness to competitive market-share losses and IRA-driven pricing pressure. Imbruvica’sdecline remained the primary drag on the oncology business, partially offsetting growth across the rest of the portfolio. AbbVie’s newer oncology products continued to demonstrate strong momentum. Ovarian cancer drug Elahere recorded sales of $224 million, up 31.2% year over year, while lymphoma drug Epkinly generated revenues of $108 million, increasing 60.8%. The broader Other Oncology category also contributed to growth, with sales reaching $39 million, more than doubling year over year and rising from $33 million in the previous quarter. Growth across these products helped counter the impact of Imbruvica’s continued erosion. AbbVie did not provide any separate updates on the commercial uptake of ovarian cancer therapy Elahere and Decnupaz, its rare blood cancer drug approved in the second quarter of 2026. The company also did not disclose individual product contributions within the Other Oncology category. Meanwhile, AbbVie is focused on expanding its oncology portfolio. Last month, the company submitted a regulatory filing seeking approval for the investigational second-generation BCMA x CD3 bispecific antibody, etentamig, for the treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. If approved, a potential launch is expected in 2027. AbbVie raised its full-year 2026 oncology revenue guidance to $6.6 billion, reflecting higher sales expectations for Venclexta, partially offset by a reduction in its Imbruvica outlook. The company now expects Venclexta sales of $3.1 billion and Imbruvica sales of $2.1 billion for 2026. Continued growth in Venclexta, Elahere and Epkinly, along with the potential launches of etentamig and the expansion of Epkinly into frontline DLBCL in 2027, could support the oncology franchise’s growth prospects. However, the pace of Imbruvica’s erosion and the commercial execution of upcoming product launches will remain important factors to watch. Other bigger players in the oncology space include AstraZeneca AZN, Merck MRK and Pfizer PFE. For AstraZeneca, oncology sales accounted for 47% of total revenues in the first nine months of 2026, driven by the strong performance of medicines such as Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Calquence and Enhertu (in partnership with Daiichi Sankyo). Merck’s oncology franchise accounted for 55% of its total revenues, led by its PD-L1 inhibitor Keytruda. In contrast, Pfizer’s oncology segment accounts for nearly 27% of its topline, driven by drugs like Padcev, Lorbrena and the Braftovi-Mektovi combination. Shares of AbbVie have gained 29% so far this year compared with the industry’s 23% growth, as seen in the chart below. From a valuation standpoint, AbbVie is trading at a discount to the industry. Based on the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, the company’s shares currently trade at 18.54 times forward 12-month earnings, below the industry average of 19.20 times. The bottom-line estimate per share for 2026 has risen from $13.94 to $13.99, while the 2027 estimate has increased from $15.95 to $16.08 over the past 30 days.
